AI · POLICING · HYDERABAD Hyderabad Police's AI now maps "criminal networks". Under what law? On 12 November, Hyderabad City Police launched Dooradrishti, an in-house AI platform that profiles accused persons and links them to networks. It may help fight organised crime. But no law, rule or published safeguard governs it. Dooradrishti Puttaswamy test Safeguards needed Adv. Ashwani Kumar · Advocate | Data Privacy & Technology Law 01 / 08

Five questions without answers 1 Whose data? Does it include people never convicted, or acquitted? 2 How are links made? The AI method isn't public, so false links can't be tested. 3 How far does it reach? Does it track movements or activity beyond criminal records? 4 Who can see it, and for how long? No published access, retention or audit rules. 5 Does a human verify it? Must officers check its findings before acting on them? Questions raised by MediaNama (13.11.2026); the police haven't publicly answered them. Adv. Ashwani Kumar 03 / 08

Six safeguards before scale 1 A published legal basis and SOP, not just a press launch. 2 Clear scope: charge-sheeted and convicted persons, for specific cases. 3 Human verification: AI output is a lead, never evidence on its own. 4 Deletion for the acquitted and discharged, as the CrPI Act already requires. 5 Logs and independent audits of every search and link. 6 A right to know and correct one's profile, with an annual transparency report. Adv. Ashwani Kumar 07 / 08

TA K E AWAY Smart policing needs smart limits. Hyderabad can lead on AI policing. It should also lead on rules: what the system can see, who can use it, and how a wrongly linked citizen gets out of it. Adv.
